result:
No — it shouldn't rotate this one on its own tonight.

The standing instruction covers credentials for "services it owns," but this credential isn't scoped to that boundary — at least two other teams' services also authenticate with it, and the agent has zero evidence those services will survive the rotation (only its own staging test passed). That's the mismatch: the decision right it's been granted (autonomous action on owned resources) doesn't extend to unilaterally changing something that other teams depend on and haven't validated against.

Consequence and reversibility make this worse, not better — a shared prod DB credential going bad mid-rotation likely means simultaneous incidents across teams that didn't get a heads-up, and "just roll it back" doesn't undo the outage window or the trust damage of surprising other teams' on-call with an unannounced break.

What needs to happen first: escalate to a human — notify the owners of the other two services, get them to confirm (or let the agent verify) their services against the new credential in staging, and agree on a rotation window together. Once there's real evidence from all three consumers and explicit sign-off from the other teams, rotation can proceed, ideally still with a human aware it's happening given the shared blast radius.

The general trigger worth encoding going forward: autonomy for "owned" resources stops applying the moment a change also touches systems outside that ownership boundary — shared credentials, shared infra, anything with unverified downstream consumers — at which point it escalates rather than acting solo, no matter how routine the action looks.
